chunks.title: CLO Master Express Lesson 26 | Techniques for Building and Rendering High-Fidelity Scenes
chunks.content: ## Overview of Building and Rendering Real Scenes in CLO 7.0 This section introduces the process of constructing and rendering high-fidelity 3D scenes using CLO's cloud-based environment and assets. Key terminology includes virtual models, scene boards, FBX model import, texture and hairline stickers, particle diameter settings, and Connect (CLO’s asset marketplace). --- ## Scene Setup and Virtual Model Reference Before building a scene, load a virtual model as a reference. In this example, the new virtual model “Yuna” by Claude is used. - Create a large board to serve as the ground, approximately one-fourth of the screen size. - Adjust the board’s particle diameter to 700 (maximum value) to exclude it from physics calculations, improving simulation performance. - Center the board in the 3D window by rotating and moving it to the ground center. This board functions as the foundational plane for the entire 3D scene. --- ## Organizing and Using Scene Materials Materials for the scene are organized into folders containing: 1. Scene model folders (Scene 1 and Scene 2) 2. JDR environment stickers (used for texturing) 3. Continuous pattern files for ground and environmental mapping These materials will be shared via WeChat public account with the keyword “live material.” --- ## Importing and Texturing FBX Models Models are imported as FBX files into the 3D window by dragging and dropping, then setting the import type to “increase” and object type to “copy.” This method allows for easy duplication and reuse of models. - Imported models may appear rough or dark due to default colors. - Apply texture stickers (color maps) and hairline stickers (fine detail maps) from the provided folders. - Adjust model color as needed to blend with the scene environment. - Use the attribute processor to uniformly scale the model by setting the X, Y, and Z ratios to the same value (e.g., 3500). - Position models using world coordinate axis tools for accurate placement on the ground. - Use the model locator’s transform handles to adjust length, width, and height independently for scene variation. --- ## Positioning and Copying Models for Scene Variation - Use right-click copy and paste to duplicate models efficiently. - Move models using keyboard shortcuts (2, 4, 6, 8) for orthogonal translation. - Rotate and scale models to create natural rhythm and variation in the scene. - Adjust the ground board's height slightly downward to avoid uneven terrain issues. --- ## Adjusting Unit Scale and Model Size - Ensure the ratio unit is set to centimeters rather than millimeters to avoid importing models too small. - After scaling, confirm the model remains centered in world coordinates. - Apply textures and hairline stickers post-import to enhance realism. - Modify model colors to harmonize with the environment (e.g., adjusting white models to warmer earth tones). --- ## Creating Terrain Variation with Models - Use specific models as parts of the ground to create height variation rather than flat terrain.

chunks.title: CLO Master Express Lesson 26 | Techniques for Building and Rendering High-Fidelity Scenes
chunks.content: --- ## Adjusting Unit Scale and Model Size - Ensure the ratio unit is set to centimeters rather than millimeters to avoid importing models too small. - After scaling, confirm the model remains centered in world coordinates. - Apply textures and hairline stickers post-import to enhance realism. - Modify model colors to harmonize with the environment (e.g., adjusting white models to warmer earth tones). --- ## Creating Terrain Variation with Models - Use specific models as parts of the ground to create height variation rather than flat terrain. - Scale terrain models up significantly (e.g., 5000 to 8000 units) and adjust vertical displacement using 3D texture adjustment axes. - Duplicate terrain models and arrange them symmetrically or asymmetrically to add natural shape variation. - Use curve lines in texture files to enhance terrain contours after removing textures, maintaining visible terrain shape. --- ## Low-Polygon Models for Performance Optimization - The shared models have low polygon counts, allowing many models to be added without significant performance loss. - This enables the creation of dense scenes with trees, rocks, plants, and accessories while maintaining efficient grid usage. --- ## Building Forest and Natural Elements - Import tree models with textures and hairline stickers; adjust scale and position to create a layered forest effect. - Use a variety of tree sizes and shapes to add depth and realism. - Position fallen and rotten trees near standing trees for natural scene composition. - Adjust color and brightness of models to match the overall scene tone. --- ## Importing and Positioning Decorative Elements - Add stone bridges, stone lamps, and other props, matching textures and colors to integrate with existing models. - Scale props appropriately to maintain scene proportion. - Place smaller decorative elements (e.g., mushrooms, flowers, grasses) strategically to enrich scene detail. - Use copy-paste and locator tools to position these elements naturally (e.g., mushrooms around tree bases). --- ## Grass, Flowers, and Small Plants - Import plant models from designated folders containing FBX files. - Adjust model colors from gray to white before applying textures. - Use stickers from the texture folder to ensure correct appearance. - Vary plant sizes to create contrast and natural growth patterns. - Position plants in gaps between stones, on tree trunks, and across the terrain using locator and scaling tools. - Introduce flowers and multi-headed plants with appropriate scaling and color adjustment. - Distribute flowers randomly around the scene, avoiding placement directly under primary models. --- ## Mushroom Group Placement and Adjustment - Import FBX files of mushroom groups, then separate individual mushrooms by moving them out. - Adjust size and color to blend with surrounding environment. - Place mushrooms near rotten trees and under canopy shadows. - Use copy-paste to distribute mushrooms evenly, avoiding unnatural clustering. - Adjust mushroom brightness to avoid visual mismatch with the scene. --- ## CLO Connect: Asset Marketplace Usage - Connect is CLO’s cloud-based asset marketplace accessible from the library panel in the software.

chunks.content: --- ## Mushroom Group Placement and Adjustment - Import FBX files of mushroom groups, then separate individual mushrooms by moving them out. - Adjust size and color to blend with surrounding environment. - Place mushrooms near rotten trees and under canopy shadows. - Use copy-paste to distribute mushrooms evenly, avoiding unnatural clustering. - Adjust mushroom brightness to avoid visual mismatch with the scene. --- ## CLO Connect: Asset Marketplace Usage - Connect is CLO’s cloud-based asset marketplace accessible from the library panel in the software. - Users can log in with their CLO account to browse, download, and upload models, clothing, shoes, and accessories. - Assets are organized into categories such as costumes, shoes, and hairstyles. - Downloaded assets can be added directly to the scene and adjusted accordingly. - Requires the latest version of CLO (7.0.358 or higher) for full functionality. - Free and paid assets are available, with free assets clearly marked. --- ## Clothing and Accessories Integration - Download and import clothing models from Connect. - Adjust particle diameter of clothing to optimize simulation speed. - Change clothing colors and materials as needed. - Add shoe models and adjust their colors and postures. - Use simulation tools to test clothing movement. - Assign actions and poses to models using the blending window for preview. --- ## Lighting Setup and Rendering Techniques This section covers lighting setup in CLO to produce realistic rendered scenes using HDR images, skylight, square lights, ball lights, and camera lens settings. ### HDR Environment Lighting - Load HDR images (high dynamic range) to simulate environmental lighting. - HDR images contain lighting and environmental data for accurate scene illumination. - Activate skylight display to show HDR background in the 3D window. - Adjust HDR intensity to brighten or darken the ambient light. - Use 360-degree HDR images and adjust camera lens angle to view lighting effects from multiple perspectives. ### Adding Square Lights - Square lights simulate large-area light sources, similar to sunlight. - Position square lights in front or above models to emphasize key elements like clothing. - Adjust square light size (e.g., 2000 mm or 2 meters) to cover the target area. - Modify intensity and turn off visible light display if necessary. - Change light color to create mood, e.g., warm yellow for early morning. - Rotate and reposition lights to create directional shadows and highlights. ### Adding Ball Lights and Accent Lighting - Ball lights simulate localized point light sources (e.g., lanterns, lamps). - Place ball lights inside props like stone lamps to create glowing effects. - Adjust radius and brightness to simulate realistic light spread. - Use multiple ball lights to enhance atmospheric depth. - Change ball light colors (e.g., warm yellow for candlelight effect). ### Camera Lens and Rendering Settings - Adjust camera lens focal length (15mm, 35mm, 40mm) to control scene depth and perspective. - Longer focal lengths (e.g., 40mm) produce a sense of distance and depth. - Modify field of view based on scene requirements.

Longer focal lengths (e.g., 40mm) produce a sense of distance and depth. - Modify field of view based on scene requirements. - Use synchronization rendering to preview lighting and scene effects in real time. --- ## Scene Composition and Final Adjustments - Combine all elements: ground, terrain variation, trees, props, plants, and lighting. - Adjust positions, rotations, and scales to create natural, rhythmic variations. - Use keyboard shortcuts and locator tools for precise movements. - Save project files frequently to avoid data loss. - Save rendering properties separately (File > Save As > Rendering Properties) to preserve lighting and camera settings for reuse. --- ## Additional Resources and Recommendations - For downloading additional models and assets, use Quick Bridge software, which offers a variety of Chinese and international models including buildings, food, and historical architecture. - Quick Bridge can be found on Bilibili and other platforms. - Follow the CLO WeChat public account and use the keyword “live material” to receive material files for practice. - CLO’s Connect marketplace is updated regularly with new models, clothing, shoes, and accessories. - Use the latest CLO software version for best compatibility and access to new features. --- ## Summary This guide covers comprehensive steps for building a realistic scene in CLO 7.0, focusing on: - Scene setup using virtual models and large ground boards. - Importing and texturing FBX models with stickers. - Creating terrain variation through scaled models and curve lines. - Efficient scene composition with model copying, positioning, and scaling. - Detailed addition of natural elements: trees, rocks, grass, flowers, and mushrooms. - Using CLO Connect for asset acquisition. - Clothing integration and simulation adjustments. - Advanced lighting techniques using HDR, skylight, square lights, and ball lights. - Camera lens adjustments for depth and perspective control. - Best practices for saving and managing project files and rendering settings. This structured approach enables users to create visually rich, high-fidelity 3D

Move models using keyboard shortcuts (2, 4, 6, 8) for orthogonal translation. - Rotate and scale models to create natural rhythm and variation in the scene. - Adjust the ground board's height slightly downward to avoid uneven terrain issues. --- ## Adjusting Unit Scale and Model Size - Ensure the ratio unit is set to centimeters rather than millimeters to avoid importing models too small. - After scaling, confirm the model remains centered in world coordinates. - Apply textures and hairline stickers post-import to enhance realism. - Modify model colors to harmonize with the environment (e.g., adjusting white models to warmer earth tones). --- ## Creating Terrain Variation with Models - Use specific models as parts of the ground to create height variation rather than flat terrain. - Scale terrain models up significantly (e.g., 5000 to 8000 units) and adjust vertical displacement using 3D texture adjustment axes. - Duplicate terrain models and arrange them symmetrically or asymmetrically to add natural shape variation. - Use curve lines in texture files to enhance terrain contours after removing textures, maintaining visible terrain shape. --- ## Low-Polygon Models for Performance Optimization - The shared models have low polygon counts, allowing many models to be added without significant performance loss. - This enables the creation of dense scenes with trees, rocks, plants, and accessories while maintaining efficient grid usage. --- ## Building Forest and Natural Elements - Import tree models with textures and hairline stickers; adjust scale and position to create a layered forest effect. - Use a variety of tree sizes and shapes to add depth and realism. - Position fallen and rotten trees near standing trees for natural scene composition. - Adjust color and brightness of models to match the overall scene tone. --- ## Importing and Positioning Decorative Elements - Add stone bridges, stone lamps, and other props, matching textures and colors to integrate with existing models. - Scale props appropriately to maintain scene proportion. - Place smaller decorative elements (e.g., mushrooms, flowers, grasses) strategically to enrich scene detail. - Use copy-paste and locator tools to position these elements naturally (e.g., mushrooms around tree bases). --- ## Grass, Flowers, and Small Plants - Import plant models from designated folders containing FBX files. - Adjust model colors from gray to white before applying textures. - Use stickers from the texture folder to ensure correct appearance. - Vary plant sizes to create contrast and natural growth patterns. - Position plants in gaps between stones, on tree trunks, and across the terrain using locator and scaling tools. - Introduce flowers and multi-headed plants with appropriate scaling and color adjustment. - Distribute flowers randomly around the scene, avoiding placement directly under primary models. --- ## Mushroom Group Placement and Adjustment - Import FBX files of mushroom groups, then separate individual mushrooms by moving them out. - Adjust size and color to blend with surrounding environment. - Place mushrooms near rotten trees and under canopy shadows. - Use copy-paste to distribute mushrooms evenly, avoiding unnatural clustering. - Load HDR images (high dynamic range) to simulate environmental lighting. - HDR images contain lighting and environmental data for accurate scene illumination. - Activate skylight display to show HDR background in the 3D window. - Adjust HDR intensity to brighten or darken the ambient light. - Use 360-degree HDR images and adjust camera lens angle to view lighting effects from multiple perspectives. ### Adding Square Lights - Square lights simulate large-area light sources, similar to sunlight. - Position square lights in front or above models to emphasize key elements like clothing. - Adjust square light size (e.g., 2000 mm or 2 meters) to cover the target area. - Modify intensity and turn off visible light display if necessary. - Change light color to create mood, e.g., warm yellow for early morning. - Rotate and reposition lights to create directional shadows and highlights. ### Adding Ball Lights and Accent Lighting - Ball lights simulate localized point light sources (e.g., lanterns, lamps). - Place ball lights inside props like stone lamps to create glowing effects. - Adjust radius and brightness to simulate realistic light spread. - Use multiple ball lights to enhance atmospheric depth. - Change ball light colors (e.g., warm yellow for candlelight effect). ### Camera Lens and Rendering Settings - Adjust camera lens focal length (15mm, 35mm, 40mm) to control scene depth and perspective. -
